items.title: BioWare Co-Founder Speaks Out on Studio Closure, Mass Effect Cancellation
items.excerpt: BioWare co-founder Greg Zeschuk has spoken out about the closure of BioWare last week, which saw 50 jobs lost as part of 400 cuts across the company, along with the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, which we've now come to learn (via a leaked internal trailer) was called Mass Effect: Universe.
items.content_text: BioWare co-founder Greg Zeschuk has spoken out about the closure of BioWare last week, which saw 50 jobs lost as part of 400 cuts across the company, along with the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, which we've now come to learn (via a leaked internal trailer ) was called Mass Effect: Universe. Speaking to 80 Level , Zeschuk lamented the end of the studio but said he went through his own emotional goodbye to the studio after he and fellow co-founder Ray Muzyka departed it on their own terms back in 2012, several months after the launch of Mass Effect 3. “I've kind of gone through all the emotions like long, long ago,” he said. “You have to break from it and kind of go, ‘OK, I've had my emotional moment.’” He continued: “I'm just at a point in my life where I've got my own other business,” he said. “My [beer] brewing business is going really well. I've got a whole other thing I'm doing, and I'm not sentimental or nostalgic. I'm kind of, like, that chapter's closed.” That said, he certainly had opinions regarding the closure of the great RPG studio he helped build. “I’m not saying it doesn’t hurt and doesn’t suck," he said. "And I think it’s kind of sad. It’s actually, in some ways, saddest for the city of Edmonton, where we’re from, because we were kind of this beacon of hope and excitement and possibility. We showed you could do something really special in a place that was not known for doing things like that.” Regarding the Saudi Public Investment Fund's $55 private buyout of EA, Zeschuk said he wasn't surprised that BioWare was ultimately shut down. “I think it was the final nail in the coffin,” he said. “I think that was the crux of it in a sense. Once again it's a completely different company now... BioWare makes these kind of unusual games that take a long time and they're complicated and so it's easier just to pump out sports games every year and that's a better business model in some ways.” Zeschuk wasn't shy about his feelings on executives without any game-development experience owning and running game development studios. “There’s this weird belief that you can just kind of recreate great games with random people and AI. It doesn’t work,” he proclaimed. “The other harsh reality of almost all these companies, the people that go down the business track never really come from the development track. Because none of these people have ever made a game, like, never really sat and made one, like, from start to finish, even a small thing, they just don’t know how it works.” Public reactions to the closure of BioWare and cancellation of Mass Effect have been strong. Here at IGN, I wrote about how BioWare was the greatest RPG developer ever , Jackie Thomas lamented that BioWare will never get the chance to redeem itself after Mass Effect Andromeda, and Matt Purslow wrote that EA never really knew what it had with BioWare. Meanwhile, composer Austin Wintory revealed he'd been in discussions with EA and BioWare about composing the soundtrack for Mass Effect 5 and was such a fan of the series that he even went so far as to release 22 minutes of Mass Effect music he'd created to help convince the publisher to hire him. And in the wider gaming public, fans expressed anger and sadness at the loss of a studio with such an incredible legacy.
items.title_en: BioWare Co-Founder Speaks Out on Studio Closure, Mass Effect Cancellation

items.title: Original Donkey Kong Poster That Was Nearly Thrown Away Sold at Auction for Record-Breaking $329,400
items.excerpt: A 1981 promotional poster for the original Donkey Kong, featuring the first public appearance of Mario, has become the the most expensive piece of original video game art ever sold at auction.
items.content_text: A 1981 promotional poster for the original Donkey Kong , featuring the first public appearance of Mario, has become the the most expensive piece of original video game art ever sold at auction. But this artwork nearly got thrown out in the garbage. According to Landry Pop Auctions, who facilitated the sale, a former Nintendo of America employee named Donna Darbous saved the poster from a collection of materials that were marked for disposal. The poster was drawn by artist Leslie Cabarga as an arcade flyer for Nintendo of America, depicting Donkey Kong angrily hoisting a barrel over his head as a determined Mario — then simply named ‘Jumpman’ — makes his way up a building to save Pauline, who cowers in fear behind her hulking captor. As told in a press release shared with IGN, this flyer has now sold for an eye-watering $329,400, making it the most expensive video game artwork ever sold at auction. That record was previously held by the original cover artwork for Prince of Persia , which sold at Heritage Auctions in 2023 for $63,000 — meaning the Donkey Kong poster blew it out of the water by a staggering $266,400. The poster inspired a sale of other historic Nintendo artworks titled Landry Pop Auctions' Jumpman: The Beginning of an Icon. This event included original production artwork from Super Mario Bros. and even some of the first illustrations of the game series’ iconic enemies. For example, original artwork of Mario and Luigi from Super Mario Bros. sold for $17,080, which Landry Pop Auctions said was nearly three times its estimate of $6,000. Original artwork of a Goomba, an ever-recurring enemy in the Mario games, raked in $10,370, more than double its $5,000 estimate. A first-production 1985 copy of Super Mario Bros. for the NES , boasting an 8.0 grading from PSA, went for $34,160, while a curious piece of history, a Nintendo of America employee orientation VHS tape that featured Mario, was also sold in this auction for $3,660 against its $1,500 estimate. "Long before Mario became the face of a multibillion-dollar entertainment franchise, he was a character on an arcade flyer. The $329,400 result is a striking reminder of how far Nintendo's most famous plumber has come, and how valuable the surviving artwork from his earliest days has become," Landry Pop Auctions said in a press release. This is the latest game-related auction sale to raise eyebrows after a retired decorator in the UK sold their collection of Pokemon cards for $2 million earlier this month. And in June, a PSA-graded 9.6 A++ copy of Super Mario Bros. for the NES was sold at auction for a record-breaking $3 million , becoming the most expensive video game in history. Image Credits: Nintendo of America, Landry Pop Auctions

items.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ Review
items.excerpt: A bigger and better version of Call of Duty's extraction shooter mode.
items.content_text: This is a standalone review that covers only Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ mode. You can find our campaign and multiplayer review here . Extraction shooters can feel a little like a modern trend, with some heavy hitters like Marathon and Arc Raiders shaking the table within the last year or so, but they’ve been a growing experiment in the shooter space for the past decade or so. Call of Duty dabbled in it with the original DMZ back in 2022 (you could even argue they were late to the party by then), and its return in 2026 is timely. I’ve logged quite a few bootsteps through the bombed out streets, scattered woodlands, and high security bases of this big new mode over the last week, and after hours of vehicle hijacking, SAM site hacking, and target elimination, I can say this bigger, better DMZ is a welcome newcomer to the extraction shooter slate. The PvPvE dynamic of extraction shooters often lives and dies by how well the mission and level design encourages you to explore, rewards you for overcoming challenges, and guides you to interact with others in order to keep those spoils. The fictional Korean Hajin region your exploits take place in is well suited for this. Its dense pockets of urban development – a village in the north, the dangerous main city in the east, an isolated prison out west – are separated by rocky forests concealing all sorts of militarized checkpoints and other points of interest hiding loot to shove into your pockets. Parts of it look a little samey, the consequence of modern urban development where (at least from the outside) most buildings look the same, especially compared to some of DMZ’s big sci-fi competitors that go above and beyond to look striking at first glance. But the map is so big that you could spend the entirety of your approximately half-hour runs in only a fraction of it. And where Battle Royales (like CoD’s own Warzone) move players around by having an encroaching death cloud forcing everyone into a smaller and smaller area, DMZ instead entices squads to adventure with its Dynamic Operations. Dynamic Ops are spontaneous missions that appear as you travel across the battlefield which come in lots of forms, from securing a package to blowing up a target to escorting a VIP. Many of them are multi-stage affairs that have your fireteam moving from point to point as NPC enemies ramp up a more coordinated defense against you. These all get rewarded by supply drops that grant you loot, the value of which escalates based on how many of them you successfully complete. I prefer this sort of objective chasing to the more standard task lists in other games like this (which also exist here, in fairness) because it makes for more engaging individual runs. I’ll prepare the best I can beforehand, but can’t be ready for every possible string of operations once I deploy. There are many actions and events, like aforementioned supply drops, that are broadcast to everyone within earshot, hypothetically to tempt other players to be nosy (and potentially belligerent). Despite those lures, open skirmishes with others have been pretty limited, as I’ve found most people opt to mind their own business. The influx of players at launch hasn't really changed the main emphasis on the E in the PvPvE structure of these runs, though human enemies can regularly play spoiler to otherwise solid runs if you’re not diligent. There was a base level of tension with every step I took or round I let off. It would be a mistake to confuse passivity with pacifism – this isn’t the Arc Raiders playerbase, which spent many of the opening months of that game more interested in helping than hurting. Whenever another player was in eye or earshot, it was assumed that a firefight was to follow, even though there is a specific truce ping that allows you the extend the olive branch to other players who you know are around but can’t (or don't want to) see in person. Like in all extraction shooters, the most tense PVP moment in DMZ happens when you’re waiting for your ride home and other players have decided that the extraction heli isn’t big enough for the both of you. Hajin is a pretty lively place. Enemy patrols speed down roadways, sometimes as lone jeeps and other times in large caravans. Helicopters and drones streak across the sky looking for interlopers like me, or occasionally other NPCs from rival factions tearing the map apart. A train runs on a schedule, and you can absolutely hitch a ride on it to get from place to place. Squads of enemies could be posted up anywhere. Weird exploding robot dogs can sniff you out as you slink from building to building. There was always at least a base level of tension with every step I took or round I let off, because there was just enough going on around me that any push I made could be the one that knocked over the house of cards I was hiding behind. Clashes with the NPC denizens of the DMZ start pretty tame, but ramp up as you and your squad make yourself more notorious by killing enemies and completing objectives. As enemy units start to don armor, pull up in more durable vehicles, and use higher grade weaponry to take you down, firefights can get desperate quickly. There's an instinct for people in pick-up groups to run out on their own, potentially to get first dibs on loot perhaps, and they almost always regret it – it doesn’t take much for enemies to get the drop on you, as you are only where you are and they are potentially anywhere and everywhere else. Lieutenants are high-level boss challenges that really stand out as maybe the single most difficult thing you can attempt during any given run. They exist in specific regions, but where one in the forests lies in wait for unsuspecting operators to pass through their zone before springing their assault, another is dressed head to toe in armor with a mini-gun and will roam a piece of the city in hopes to stop you mid mission. They are better off avoided unless you’ve brought high-end gear with the specific purpose of hunting them. The secret sauce of what makes the extraction shooter so appealing is the level of agency each player has to play how they want in a higher stakes PvP setting. You can go into every encounter guns blazing, or you can tip toe through them, taking the long way and hopefully having your patience and preparation rewarded. You can make racking up “objective completes” and bagging top tier loot your mission, or you can try to hunt down every human player you can. I like engaging in a bit of PvP, but my nearly 40-year-old eyes and reflexes frankly can’t keep up with the kind batshit action that goes on in the standard multiplayer modes (or even Warzone). In contrast, DMZ has created a great sandbox that serves all varieties of playstyles adequately. There's always a way to jam up sightlines or to find some cover and take a breath. Every building has multiple points of entry, so sieges or chases through them always require some level of decision making. Sub-missions are always an option, where you can hack a tower for a UAV scan or SAM site coverage to support you in your main objective, but only if you’re willing the take on the added risk. I always felt like I could “yes, and” what was happening at any given moment, and thats not true for many of DMZ’s contemporaries. Call of Duty’s top tier military shooter gunplay feels at home in DMZ. Call of Duty’s top tier military shooter gunplay, toeing the line between the lethality of simulations and the snappy speed of arcadey romps, feels at home in DMZ as well. All of the new tweaks, like the way your weapons interact with your surroundings or movement adjustments, feel like they had roaming gunfights in an open world in mind. Being able to cancel out of mantles so you aren’t stuck in an animation when you least want to be feels like the kind of quality of life inclusion that Warzone demonstrated was needed for a long time. That said, the smattering of guns lack much in the way of real identities outside of the normal archetypal framings that have existed in gaming forever (shotgun, assault rifle, sniper, etc.). You can also drop into story missions, which are quest chains that include more structure, resembling the campaign missions without the more cinematic story elements. These were pretty rowdy and unique, like an escort mission where our squad had to wheel an injured general out of a hospital, bed and all, while enduring swarms of enemy combatants. There's a finite number of these and the possible rewards are more limited, with less incentive to explore the places around you and no enemy players to pirate or evade. But they serve as a great tasting platter of the pace Dynamic Ops keep and a good tour of the various locations on the map you'll need to get familiar with. In between missions, you’ll tend to all of your gear and progression from the safety of your FOB. Weapons, crafting ingredients, and consumables that you procure out in the field can be sorted through here, all of it put at risk when you equip it and redeploy. When you unlock the 3D printer and gunsmith areas, crafting new toys and upgrading weapons becomes the main way you spend your plunder to enhance your chances in Hajin. You can easily blow tens of thousands of won to trick out a weapon, but I found that the investments can be worth it in order to differentiate playstyles, like if you want a quieter load out with suppressors or a certain sort of optics to make mid-to-long range encounters more beneficial. I didn’t find the more money I invested automatically made my loadout feel more powerful, though. Gaining experience is pretty easy as everything you do in the field gives you some amount of it. Progressing through the account level unlocks list was pretty breezy at first, helpful because a lot of recipes for some core equipment like grenades and ammo boxes are early rewards. At around half way up I found things slowed down quite significantly, but I also didn't find many late level goals to be enticing enough to turn up the grind. There's powerful kit, like a pistol that you can shoot downed teammates with to revive them, but I'm not torching all my spare time to sprint to level 64 to get it. Similarly, Operators have individual sets of trait trees that you upgrade with points they earn in the field. These don’t appear to be novel to any individual fighter; there's no Ghost-specific ability where he gets unique buffs while saying something very British. Instead there are pools of passive traits across three categories, all operators have a choice between the same handful of major traits, and the 15 or so minor traits that fill out the trees are randomized. What makes an operator special seems to be limited mostly to how they look and sound, which was a bit of a bummer. I was never champing at the bit to get my build “right.” These traits can be meaningful in the field, though. One of the randomized traits I acquired for Valeria, Ammo Scavenger, doubled the ammo I got from ammo packs and made conserving my shots basically a thing of the past. The faster revive speed all operators have access to in their Survivalist tree has been the difference between clutch plays and total wipes on more than one occasion. There's definitely some kind of character building to be had here, but you really can’t know where it’s all leading until the next group of traits to choose from are revealed. And all that is before accounting for the fact that there's no way to reset or reallocate these trait points outside of abandoning the operator all together if you fail to extract with them (as opposed to spending some cash to get them back into the fight). All of this created an environment where I was never champing at the bit to get my build “right.” Everything I picked worked at least a little bit. But I was also pretty detached from the whole process once I realized you really only had one shot at it per operator. I haven't maxed out any operator skill trees or account level reward path yet, but there are no substantial carrots left to tempt me down them either. Regardless of the trait investment, how good or bad I did in a run came down to how few bullets I ate in the process, and these trees, though valuable in specific cases, really didn't change that.
items.title_en: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ Review

items.title: Kane Parsons Confirms Meetings With Valve, But Won't Adapt Their Games If It Can't Be Done Right
items.excerpt: Backrooms director Kane Parsons has confirmed he has had meetings with Valve, but he has no plans to adapt any of their IP if it can't be done well.
items.content_text: Backrooms director Kane Parsons has confirmed his meetings with Valve, but says that he has no plans to adapt any of their games if it can't be done well. When speaking on an October 28 episode of The Kyle Buchanan Show , Parsons wore a Valve hoodie, which prompted Buchanan to inquire about Parsons' recent trips to the developer's corporate offices. (Following the release of Backrooms, the director noted that he wanted to make a Portal movie and subsequently posted about trips to Valve on Instagram .) Naturally, Parsons didn't confirm or deny what exactly is going on between them, but confirmed that he has had conversations with the company — but he only wants to work with them if it's done right. "They work in experiments, and I like that, because that tends to be how I work," he said. "I don't have a desire to sensationalize anything I may or may not be talking to them about over there, because it's mainly: Is it possible to make something compelling in some way that we like? What do you guys want to do? What do I want to do? Is there anything on the table in any way, shape, or form? "And if it's not, I would defend a future where we don't even go down that road, but it's more like having an abstract creative conversation that could flow in like 30 different directions. If you know the way Valve works, I think they're looking to experiment more internally than anything that's going to be talked about. If something cool comes of it, I am sure somehow, people will know." As noted, Parsons has expressed interest in making a Portal movie and also recently confirmed that he is working on three "dream projects." These projects seem to be linked to some kind of IP, but Parsons has also previously stated he has no real interest in a property like Star Wars, and his desire for adaptations lies more within a small handful of things from his childhood, such as Valve's games. Whether a Portal movie actually happens remains to be seen, but it's good to hear that Parsons isn't simply trying to jack the franchise from Valve. Although there hasn't been a new mainline Portal game since 2011, interest in the series remains high among fans. Perhaps a film could inspire a new game... or maybe Parsons has ambitions beyond a movie and would like to do something with the game's developers, instead. He has extensive experience with Blender, so he isn't out of his element, after all.

items.title: James Gunn Confirms Batman and Wonder Woman Are 'Diamond Characters' in the DCU Despite Their Continued Absence
items.excerpt: James Gunn has clarified DC Studios’ 8-10 year roadmap and confirmed its focus on Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman as its “diamond characters.”
items.content_text: James Gunn has clarified DC Studios’ 8-10 year roadmap and confirmed its focus on Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman as its “diamond characters.” Gunn shared this information on Threads in response to a now-deleted post, where he urged the original poster to study up on his quotes from January 2023 in regards to what his version of the DCU will end up looking like. “I said some stories would be standalone like the Guardians movies were (which is what Clayface is), and some stories would have part of a larger narrative structure, which is what the Superman Saga is. All that said, each piece of the larger story should work on its own with or without having to see everything else,” he said. He went on to clarify that the “often-cited 8-10 year roadmap” for the DCU doesn’t just apply to story points, but also outlines the plan for “DC as a whole.” This includes focusing on “diamond characters,” which Gunn confirmed are, perhaps unsurprisingly, Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman, as well as “smaller characters we could turn into diamonds.” These smaller characters were listed as Krypto the Superdog, John Stewart, and Peacemaker. According to Gunn, this plan also factors in how DC will “foster filmmaker freedom and allow for multiple tones and ratings, the influences of Star Wars and George R.R. Martin, and so much more." “It's exciting seeing things start to come together, and all that makes me even more excited for what we have in store for everyone in Man of Tomorrow,” he said. It’s encouraging to see Gunn confirm that Batman and Wonder Woman are still a big focus for his DCU, given that we haven’t seen hide nor hair of Wonder Woman and barely a glimpse of Batman’s silhouette in the animated Creature Commandos series. Thus far, the only “diamond character” mentioned in this specific post that has been featured in Gunn’s DCU is Superman. Elsewhere, the Lanterns and Clayface have finally gotten some love (with Lanterns receiving rave reviews , though audience opinions on Clayface have been a mixed bag ), and The People v. Gorilla Grodd is also in the works. It seems that Supergirl wasn’t mentioned as either a “diamond character” or a character that could be turned "into a diamond" in Gunn's post — though, given that she had her own movie, it’s safe to assume that she has firmly established her place in the DCU hierarchy as a central figure. Batman is another story altogether. Unrelated to Matt Reeves’ The Batman movies, the DCU’s take on the caped crusader has yet to be revealed; while Alan Ritchson was a popular pick from fans, DC Studios boss Peter Safran has stated they still haven’t found the right role for him to play. Batman is set to have his own movie in the DCU, titled The Brave and the Bold , which is in the works but has no official release date. Where Wonder Woman fits in Gunn’s DCU is just as nebulous. Similarly, no casting has been confirmed for this part, though fans are convinced that Adria Arjona will soon wield the Lasso of Truth on screen. It’s also unclear when, or how, she’ll be introduced to things, but Gunn has made it clear that she’s a priority. In other exciting DC news, a live-action Poison Ivy show was confirmed to be in the works earlier this month, with The Penguin showrunner Lauren LeFranc set to produce. Similarly, no casting has been confirmed (though rumors of ScarJo playing the character continue to swirl).

items.title: Outlander's Sam Heughan Hints at Role in Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum
items.excerpt: During a recent appearance at a book festival, Outlander star Sam Heughan strongly suggested that he may have a role in the upcoming film The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum.
items.content_text: Outlander star Sam Heughan has strongly suggested that he may have a role in the upcoming film The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum . Heughan spoke earlier this month at Scotland’s Wigtown Book Festival, during which the topic of J. R. R. Tolkien’s literary saga and subsequent film adaptations came up. This wouldn’t be an unusual topic to raise with Heughan, as he’s named after Samwise Gamgee and his brother, Cirdan, is named after an Elf. (Their parents belonged to a London hippie community called Gandalf's Garden.) When the moderator suggested the Lord of the Rings film franchise was “exhausted” at this point, Heughan cryptically replied, "No, it's not exhausted. I'm not giving anything away, but I may have been in New Zealand recently." You can watch the exchange for yourself below. Sam Heughan on The Hunt for Gollum https://t.co/EeVmIaxx3l — The Mellon Heads - LOTR Podcast (@mellon_heads) October 28, 2026 The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum has been filming in New Zealand under the direction of Andy Serkis . And as Winter Is Coming points out, “another eagle-eyed Outlander fan account, @samjamie_stillhere, noticed that a rare edition of The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien went up for auction to benefit the ALS Network, which was signed by ‘people who have taken his world to the screen, and people who are taking it there next.’ The list of signatures includes a number of stars and producers from The Hunt for Gollum, all of whom have their roles for the film listed... as well as Sam Heughan.” Maybe Heughan was just visiting the set of The Hunt for Gollum as a fan, or perhaps he has a heretofore undisclosed role in the film. If so, who do you think he plays? Let us know in the comments. For more coverage on all things Middle-earth, read why Jamie Dornan isn’t trying to “outdo” Viggo Mortensen's Aragorn in The Hunt for Gollum and discover why The Rings of Power Season 3 is “turning the page on the show .”

items.title: 'Appreciate the Fans' — GTA 5 Cast Tell Jason and Lucia’s Actors the Most Important Things They Should Know Before GTA 6 Launches Them to Fame
items.excerpt: The stars behind GTA 5’s Franklin, Michael, and Trevor, along with the voice of CJ from San Andreas, were asked if they had any advice for the actors playing GTA 6’s Jason and Lucia now that the game is almost here.
items.content_text: The stars behind GTA 5’s Franklin, Michael, and Trevor, along with the voice of CJ from San Andreas, were asked if they had any advice for the actors playing GTA 6’s Jason and Lucia now that the game is almost here. The long wait for GTA 6 is almost over. After 13 years, the game is finally set to release on November 19 in one of the biggest (and potentially most expensive) pop culture moments in history. Knowing just how passionate Rockstar’s fanbase can be, actors who starred in previous games in the franchise shared their words of wisdom with the as-yet unannounced actors who are playing Jason and Lucia, the dual protagonists of GTA 6, in an interview with All Out Gaming at MCM Comic Con. “Have fun,” CJ’s actor, Young Maylay, said. “To be honest, just listen to what Rockstar says,” Shawn ‘Solo’ Fonteno, famous for playing Franklin in GTA 5, added. “They’re gonna lead you in the right direction. … But get ready. That’s all I can say, is get ready. It’s a ride that they’re gonna be on for a while.” Young Maylay continued, remarking on how the GTA games have garnered dedicated fanbases from multiple generations of players. “We’ll always be the characters that we are, and for the generation of kids who are coming up, you’re gonna have certain brackets,” he said. “Right now, I got all the OGs. Everybody coming in my line — you catch some youngsters, but you got guys with the grey hair coming in saying, ‘Hey man! You’re the guy, CJ!’ And they [gesturing to the GTA 5 cast] have all the youngsters right now. So, during this time period, you’re gonna grow with your fanbase. It’s not like everything’s gonna get shut down by you guys [speaking of GTA 6]… we’ll always be those characters, and you can’t take that from us.” Ned Luke, who played Michael De Santa in GTA 5 , urged the upcoming stars to be grateful for the game’s fans. “Just make sure that you appreciate the fans. Let the fans know… fake appreciation, they can smell it. You have to really appreciate them, genuinely, because what we have is because of them. If you don’t have the fans, you don’t got nothin’. They’re the game, and that’s the bottom line,” he imparted. The cast's warm sentiments toward GTA fans is at odds with one particular star in the franchise: Steven Ogg, who infamously said he felt "nothing inside" regarding GTA 6 because he's "not a gamer" and has "never played a video game" before. That being said, he did suggest killing off his character at the beginning of GTA 6 as a means of "passing the torch" to the next era. "I think that would be cool, because it also acknowledges the fans of like, 'Hey, thank you.' Pass the torch, stomp Trevor's head in, and sort of put an end to that and allow a new generation to take over," he mused back in 2025. Thus far, the actors who play Jason and Lucia have not been officially announced, though fans are extremely convinced that they’ve discovered the gal who lent her facial features to Jason’s partner in crime. Fans suspect she will be played by an actress named Manni L. Perez , as she has the exact same voice and bears a strong resemblance with the GTA protagonist. (For her part, she’s been very careful to honor her supposed NDA, if she really is involved in the project.) The fervor around GTA 6 is at an all-time high. Rockstar is ramping up marketing for the title in a major way with a Vice City-themed takeover of Miami that includes massive signs advertising the fictional city, even partnering with the Miami Heat to give the team some Vice City uniforms for their November 18 game against the Milwaukee Bucks. Players will even get a chance to eat at one of the game’s fast food joints , Burger Shot, at the Kaseya Center while they watch the two teams face off on the court.

items.title: Ali G: Who Iz I? Review
items.excerpt: Sacha Baron Cohen’s attempt to resurrect Ali G goes disastrously off the rails, with barely a joke to be found.
items.content_text: Ali G: Who Iz I? is on Prime Video now, and maybe in a theater near you, though probably not for much longer. Once the genesis of Sacha Baron Cohen’s mockumentary career, white Rude Boy poseur Ali G now marks its whimper of an ending. Released on Prime Video just five days after its theatrical release, the actor’s directorial debut Ali G: Who Iz I? barely holds together as either cinema or practical joke — let alone where the two have met in the past, by way of his exceptionally enduring Borat. His efforts this time feel especially feeble, landing somewhere in the realm of an unfocused Matt Walsh documentary, where the result isn’t so much laughter, or even provocation, but puzzled annoyance. Fifteen minutes in, one of his unsuspecting targets sums it up succinctly when shown a presentation meant to offend her: “I don’t care.” Cohen’s latest borrows characters from both HBO’s Da Ali G show as well as his Showtime series Who Is America? in an attempt to weave a political portrait of the modern United States, all wrapped in a flimsy narrative. Like the riotous Borat sequel Subsequent Moviefilm , Who Iz I? is nominally about the wannabe British Rastafari facing fatherhood, when he learns that his longtime girlfriend Julie (Morgana Robinson, taking over for Kellie Bright from the narrative comedy Ali G Indahouse) is pregnant with their child. An attempt to get a third season of his HBO interview series off the ground finds him flying across the pond to LA, where his arrival catches the attention of another Cohen character, Showtime’s Dr. Nira Cain-N'Degeocello, an outdated send-up of liberal academia who hopes to nail him for “cultural appropriation,” despite speaking over people himself. Along the way, both characters interact with various bystanders in Cohen’s signature prankish style, but his instigations prove limp. There just doesn’t seem to be enough footage to string together a film of everyday subjects responding with outrage, indignation, or even the strained politeness underlying the original Borat from 2006. Two decades later, everyone seems bored by this commonplace, microcelebrity tomfoolery, whether or not they recognize the man behind the makeup. They mostly don’t, though at least one of them, involved in the movie’s confoundingly scattered climax, appears to have gone along with it for the daily rate. Perhaps this is why Cohen feels the need for heavy-handed explanations, in the movie’s opening and closing, of how his mockumentary format works. The caricatures Cohen portrays feel tame in comparison to a world increasingly divided by political fissures, though given how much the movie’s first half is concerned with “cancel culture” and “DEI” — things even the U.S. government uses as phantom boogeyman — the movie’s mission statement is too askew to root for in the first place. While it does eventually set its sights on those in power, it opts for low-hanging fruit in the form of penile humor that its subjects mostly ignore, forcing Cohen to cut awkwardly around non-reactions. Who Iz I? is a film that takes no risks and has nothing to say, all in service of misguided self-preservation. However, setting aside the movie’s asymmetrical political bent doesn’t yield much of interest to begin with, because Who Iz I? is really only about America on the surface. What it’s really about is Cohen, or rather Ali G, in a way that threatens to be interesting for the briefest moment. Will the character wrestle with his own irrelevance when he fails to secure airtime? Not so fast! Instead, the hamstrung plot grows increasingly obsessed with Dr. Nira’s attempts to find dirt on Ali on make him persona non grata, as though wayward online criticisms of Cohen’s shtick had gotten under his skin and he were trying to pre-empt objections to the movie through Cohen-on-Cohen discourse. If anyone was trying to silence Cohen’s comedy, they’ve clearly been unsuccessful, since he managed to make this movie — though its failures are a product of its own inability to strike while the iron is hot. A three second Cameo from Rachel Dolezal isn’t going to cut it in 2026. This is largely in line with the film’s M.O. Few gags or targets stick around long enough to let the absurdities land. The Ali G character isn’t so much deployed to prod at people’s politics as he is to be a clownish presence waving his arms for attention, while Cohen also portrays an exaggerated mishmash of what he pictures his critics are like, or what they believe. At the very least, this yields a revealing portrait of artistic insecurity, if an unintentional one. Who Iz I? is a film that takes no risks and has nothing to say, all in service of misguided self-preservation, as Cohen fails to read the tea leaves of a culture that has, for better or worse, long left him behind.
items.title_en: Ali G: Who Iz I? Review

items.title: Wendy's Is Making a Turn-Based RPG and It Actually Looks Really Good
items.excerpt: Wendy’s — yes, the American fast food chain — is releasing a surprisingly gorgeous, pixelated, turn-based RPG on Steam, and the internet is legitimately stunned by how good it looks.
items.content_text: Wendy’s — yes, the American fast food chain — is releasing a surprisingly gorgeous, pixelated, turn-based RPG on Steam, and the internet is legitimately stunned by how good it looks. The game, titled WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones, is a 2D RPG where players join Wendy in her journey to “battle evil mech-monsters to save a culinary kingdom in peril.” A trailer and screenshots for the game show Wendy and a party of three other adventurers traversing terrain fraught with food-themed obstacles and duking it out with sentient menu items. For instance, one of the enemies Wendy faces is a container full of french fries that have transformed into snake-like monsters called ‘Frydusa.’ In one gameplay still, she must find a way around a river of sauce that has spilled out from a container. The game’s dialogue seems to poke fun at itself, with Wendy saying in one screenshot, “Looks like he’s been writing notes to some guy named Baconator. No way that’s a real name.” In another, she asks, “Where’s the beef?” Of course, Wendy can use a Dave’s Single, Junior Bacon Cheeseburger, and other menu items to restore her HP during battle, where she’s joined by allies like Sir Chicken and more. The game is set to release “soon,” with no specific launch date given. It does have an official Steam page , suggesting that this isn’t just a gimmick game but an actual, fully-fledged title with real effort and intent behind it. WendyQuest is developed by 81monkeys, an independent game studio based out of Port Moody, British Columbia. They are also working on a game called World of Anterra, which is described as “an innovative open world roleplaying game” inspired by “classic and modern” titles. Thus far, reactions to Wendy’s pixelated project have been largely positive. “GOTY contender. This actually looks great,” one user joked on Twitter/X. “Wait, why does it look kind of good?” another asked . “I honestly miss fast food games....Excited to play this!” said another . Still others are pleased that no AI was used in this game’s production, despite it being, for all intents and purposes, a marketing tactic. Its Steam page proudly states that the title is “100% fresh and 100% human made.” Of course, others couldn’t help but compare it to Burger King’s infamous Sneak King game from ages long past (2006), where players could “step into the King’s royal shoes and use cunning stealth to sneak up behind unsuspecting people and bestow them with a delicious meal.” (While a novelty, it wasn't an especially 'good' game. We rated it a 6.7 out of 10 .) This isn't the first time Wendy's has made a game; in fact, it released a free, 100-page tabletop RPG back in 2019 called Feast of Legends where players could battle Ronald McDonald. I have to admit that the chain's latest game is one of the more ambitious fast food marketing tactics I’ve seen thus far, and oddly, I’m actually keen on playing it when it actually comes out. Dangit — now I’m craving a Frosty.

items.excerpt: IGN can exclusively reveal the first trailer for Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey 3, which director Scott Chambers calls “absolute carnage.” The slasher sequel will open in late January 2027.
items.content_text: IGN can exclusively reveal the first trailer for Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey 3 , which director Scott Chambers calls “absolute carnage.” You can watch the new trailer via the player above or the embed below. The film’s teaser poster can also be seen below. “After the brutal capture of Pooh, Tigger, and Rabbit by the sinister Woozles Circus, fifteen years pass and the once-feral creatures are transformed into attractions in a twisted traveling carnival run by the mysterious Karna, occult showman Shandor, and the immortal ringmaster Balthazar. Meanwhile, Momo Milne, an orphan desperate to uncover the truth about her missing mother, traces her last known whereabouts to Woozles Ltd. Alongside her outspoken best friend Billie, Momo infiltrates the circus by taking a job among its bizarre performers,” according to the official synopsis. “As the girls uncover horrifying secrets behind the spectacle—including drugged half-human creatures, disappearances, and gruesome killings hidden behind the carnival lights—Momo realizes her mother’s disappearance is tied to the circus’ darkest mystery. Drawn into a nightmare where fairy tales become blood-soaked reality, Momo must survive Pooh and his monstrous companions while uncovering the truth before she becomes the next act in Woozles’ deadly show.” The film is scripted by Richard Stanley (Color Out of Space, Dust Devil, Hardware). In a statement provided to IGN, director Scott Chambers says “Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey 3 is absolute carnage. I counted 20 character deaths during filming, and every one of them was captured practically on camera using real prosthetics, special-effects makeup and physical gore effects. I think this is a thrilling new entry in the Blood and Honey universe. It is bigger, bloodier and more ambitious, but it also plays an important part in the wider story we are building. This film leads directly towards Poohniverse: Monsters Assemble—our Avengers-style crossover—and acts as a major stepping stone towards that eventual finale.” Chambers continued, “The story reveals how these creatures became so angry, damaged and vengeful, giving audiences a deeper understanding of the monsters they have become. It also brings an exciting new character to life in Rabbit, voiced by the legendary Roger L. Jackson from Scream. His performance gives Rabbit a genuinely chilling presence, and I cannot wait for audiences to meet him.” In addition to Jackson, Chambers and Stanley are also in the cast, with Stanley playing Balthazar Von Woozle. The cast also includes Josephine Blazier, Kira Reed, Leo Harris, Zena Donnelly, and Harrison Davis. Furthermore, Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey 3 features prominent social media horror content creators Cris Parker (3C Films) and Slashertalk. The film is from Jagged Edge Productions and will be distributed by ITN Distribution in late January 2027. Stuart Alson, Nicole Holland, and Evgeny Lensky serve as Executive Producers.

items.title: Sony Channels '90s Transparent Trend With New Prism Collection of DualSense Controllers and PS5 Covers
items.excerpt: PlayStation is bringing back the '90s transparent trend with the Prism Collection, a spread of DualSense controllers and matching PS5 covers in three new colorways.
items.content_text: PlayStation is bringing back the '90s transparent trend with the Prism Collection, a spread of DualSense controllers and matching PS5 covers in three new colorways. Preorders open on November 10 at 10am local time ahead of the collection's full launch next year. The Prism Collection DualSense controllers, available in Flare Orange, Emerald Green, and Graphite Gray, are releasing globally with a recommended retail price (RRP) of $84.99 USD (€84.99/£74.99). Matching PS5 console covers have an RRP of $74.99 USD (€74.99/£64.99). A PlayStation blog post offers a closer look at the new see-through designs. The images are accompanied by insights from the design team, who were particularly “excited to bring a transparent appearance to PS5.” "We wanted to bring back the iconic see-through trend of the late '90s in a fresh, modern way that complements the PS5’s industrial design," said PlayStation designer Leo Cardoso. The blog post also highlights that the see-through casing offers a “closer look at the design and craftsmanship behind our DualSense controllers and PlayStation 5 consoles.” Fellow designer Satoshi Aoyagi describes the three colors the team chose to showcase the transparent mould: “A vibrant orange that subtly takes on a rosy hue where the transparent material overlaps, a deep hunter green that gains depth through its transparency, and a cool-toned storm gray.” The full Prism Collection will be available to preorder from PlayStation Direct and select retailers starting November 10, with the full release scheduled for February 4. Sony has released over a dozen DualSense color variants in the PS5 generation on top of limited-edition controllers tied to specific game releases like Astro Bot and Death Stranding . While the company is expanding the reach of its hardware collaborations, like a new DualSense controller with Kpop star Lisa , its most popular release of late was the 30th Anniversary PlayStation collection . With the Prism Collection, the design team appears to be doubling down on audience demand for retro designs that tap into nostalgia for classic gaming eras. PlayStation as a whole continues to be embroiled in controversies stemming from Sony's decision to cut disc production as well as a number of studio closures . Despite the backlash, Sony saw a 22% increase in PS5 sales during the past month, likely tied to the release of Insomniac’s Wolverine and the lead-up to GTA 6. Phantom Blade Zero is the next ( sort of ) PlayStation exclusive set to hit consoles, and according to our reviewer, it’s looking pretty darn good .

For starters, players can expect a physical edition of the game when it launches in 2027. That means it will beat the deadline to be published on a disc, just ahead of PlayStation's all-digital shift in 2028. The game will also boast a photo mode, which aims to be "everything you expect from a camera." They're working hard to feature all of the detailed settings you'd expect from an actual camera, such as depth of field, lighting options, filters that call back to the original films, and more. As for the team building this game, about a third of the original crew that made the first title are working on the sequel, but they were looking for big fans when interviewing staff for the initial game. Lead game designer James Green called the sequel a "dream project." Alien: Isolation 2 will be set months after the first game and, as revealed in a trailer , it will take place partially outside, which will allow the Xenomorph to behave differently. It will use the wider environment to hunt you more effectively by taking advantage of the rough weather and lack of claustrophobic environments where you can typically hear or see it coming. The team is once again trying to tap into the feeling of the original film, where a singular Xenomorph is hunting you as opposed to a whole army of them. One big feature the team is also pushing is that you can enable an option to toggle your microphone on and off. This will take whatever audio is being fed into your mic, whether it be you screaming, setting down a cup on your desk, or your dog barking, and feed it back into the game. As a result, whatever noise you make in real life could theoretically attract the Xenomorph or other threats.

items.title: How Absolute Batman #25 Changes Everything for Bruce Wayne
items.excerpt: Absolute Batman #25 closes out the series' latest storyline with a shocking twist that changes everything for Bruce Wayne. Here's what you need to know.
items.content_text: Full spoilers follow for Absolute Batman #25! Absolute Batman #25 may well be the most important chapter of this series to date. It marks the end of the "Straw Man" story arc, culminating in the long-awaited showdown between Batman and the Joker and a truly game-changing final page. This issue is such a big deal that the series is going on a short hiatus for the remainder of 2026, leaving readers to sit with these major revelations for a few months. What happens in issue #25, and how does this showdown redefine Batman's crusade going forward? Here's what you need to know. Absolute Batman Meets Absolute Joker Having finally overcome Scarecrow and his relentless campaign of psychological manipulation, this storyline ends with Batman finally venturing into Grimm Manor and preparing to confront the man they call the Joker. There, he's surprised to find not Jack Grimm, but his friends gathered in a sitting room. Waylan Jones, Eddie Nygma, Oswald Cobblepot, and Harvey Dent have all staged an intervention to convince Bruce to give up his fanatical crusade. In turn, each man admits that they were approached by Jack Grimm, who revealed that he's been secretly helping Bruce evade the authorities. Grimm provided each with evidence that his business empire is 100% legitimate, that he's been campaigning against the Ark-M facility, and that he genuinely wants to help Bruce before Bruce gets himself killed. The friends tell Bruce that he has one last chance to turn himself in for psychological treatment, or else Grimm will finally leak his identity to the authorities. Batman knows his friends have been fooled by a master manipulator, so he leaps out a window and flees into the woods with the GCPD hot on his trail. He then falls through a hole and lands in Grimm's version of the Batcave, complete with all the trophies that, in another universe, are the rightful property of Bruce himself. Grimm is waiting for Batman in his disgusting but rejuvenating cocoon of dead babies. He emerges and tells Batman how happy he is to finally have a worthy nemesis again after so many years of boredom. It's here we learn that all the costumes on display in the "Joker Cave" are those worn by warriors that Grimm bested over the years. Previously, the series suggested his origins date back to the 1800s, but it would seem he's actually far older still, possibly dating back to the Roman Empire. Joker reveals his true, monstrous form and the two men begin battling. Though Batman is able to repeatedly wound Joker with his battle ax and razor-sharp ear daggers, the villain shrugs off the damage and keeps laughing. To him, the funniest joke of all is the idea that one man thinks he can stand up to the systems of power that have existed since the dawn of civilization. Just as Joker prepares to devour Batman and cut their rivalry short, The Bat (or Barbara Gordon) shows up to give the villain a faceful of her shotgun. The two heroes plunge into the river at the depths of the Joker Cave and make their escape. Absolute Batman #25's Twist Ending The Bat brings Batman back to Harley Quinn's hideout, where they stitch up the battered hero and Batman makes peace with his jilted partner. Batman has survived his first battle with Joker, but it's become clear just how badly outmatched he is. And now he faces the possibility that Joker will escalate their feud by revealing his identity to the world (not that this hulking, 6' 9" powerhouse has ever done a particularly great job of hiding it). But even that problem takes a backseat to the stunning revelation that closes out issue #25. Bruce is suddenly reunited with Selina Kyle, who reveals she's pregnant. It seems Absolute Batman is about to become a father. One of the biggest differences between the regular and Absolute versions of Batman is that the latter has more to lose in his quest to save Gotham City. Absolute Batman still has a mother and a loving relationship with Selina. And now that difference looks to be intensified, as he's about to have a child to protect on top of everything else. The idea of Batman and Catwoman becoming parents is hardly new for DC. In the classic Earth-2 universe, the two eventually marry and raise a daughter named Helena, who grows up to become the vigilante Huntress. At one point it appeared as though DC would follow suit in its core comic book universe with Tom King's Batman series, but they've since rendered the Batman/Catwoman comic that closes out King's run as non-canon. As you'd expect, this twist is going to dramatically affect the arc of Absolute Batman's journey. Writer Scott Snyder posted on Bluesky , "It'll set the stage for the entire series going forward." More than ever, he stands to lose everything if he doesn't find a way to overcome Jack Grimm and his army of horrible creations. Let us know what you think of this latest Absolute Batman twist in the comments below. For more on the series, check out IGN's review of Absolute Batman #24 and see how the series reinvented one of Bruce Wayne's greatest tragedies . Jesse is a mild-mannered staff writer for IGN. Allow him to lend a machete to your intellectual thicket by following @jschedeen on BlueSky .
